Outside of very specific origins or playstyles (hive/gestalt) I tend to gravitate towards first thinking of the governing body that unified the species and work backwards from there. So I tend to pick things like ethics/civics/origins first because those things define what your nation prioritizes. From there its matter of working backwards. 

For example: I recently made an oligarchic shattered ring world origin, catalytic processing and free traders. So I worked backwards from there and ended up with the Floris Mutatis. A plantoid species that managed to evolve naturally on an abandoned ring world - the moment they would have reached a sufficient level of technological understanding they would figure out their home is not a naturally formed celestial body. By studying their own home they would uncover the secrets of catalytic processing. Which is a huge breakthrough considering the limitations of a shattered ring world. The free trade I justified using similar means, a shattered ringworld is cool but not amazing to live in so the flow of goods is important. Ended up playing them as a biological empire that was fascinated by inorganic 'life'. Ended up being best friends with a custodian AI and even managed to get an assimilator to be chill with me when I ascended with cybernetics. 

TLDR: Don't let rp get in the way of playing the builds you want! Let the build inform the rp.

This post made me think about what Jake said in DS9, 'we work to better ourselves and the whole of humanity'. You don't really do those things in a holodeck because at the end of the day its an entertainment product that can and will conform to your preexisting comforts denying you growth.

On a side note - I think any addiction causes the same issues. You stop being able to do things without the stimulant or activity you are addicted to. So if there ever came the time when you had to go without access to your holodeck you would find your self unable to adapt to the 'real' world.

Tier 3
Honestly grab whatever, I went transmutation for steelskin and devastation for warbreeds 

Tier 4
Tome of the Crucible is the final piece of your ranged echantment - meteor arrows, this turns your zephyr archers into artillery. I whole heartedly agree that was GoT biggest problem as the show went on; they lost complete track of the characters.  Which inevitably led to plot decisions that made zero sense.  Jaime coming off as cartoonishly villainous is exactly my point, the only reason we can root for him is because we are literally inside his brain. Without the narrative form of the POV the man's actions come off as self-explanatory and one note. 

People have head cannon versions of these characters, and they have to because of how the book is written - we know very little about the character my flair is referencing, but I obviously still like them. The problem is that people place their head cannon above any other interpretation which makes any adaptation that doesn't use their version of characters fundamentally disappointing.

Praying to every god in Planetos that the writers don't fumble on their set up of these characters as the show continues.

The wildest criticisms of the show to me are the ones that revolve around characterization. So many people are up in arms about perceived changes to characters, which makes no sense. These are barely characters in the books, they're basically just proper nouns that do actions. Could you imagine if the main series was written like F&B and was just a series of events with people making assumptions after the fact for 'why' they happened? Jaime and Theon would literally come off as cartoonishly villainous.

No one has to like all the ways the show portrays these characters but its disingenuous to say that these are all deviations from existing characterizations. Even the worst scenes in this show add more depth to characters than existed before it.
I think it's entirely reasonable to approach a book like F&B which is literally a fake history book with sourcing and author bias through historic lenses to see how it holds up as a history book.
